6940:
When you give the devil his due, you are being fair enough to admit something good or praiseworthy about a person you strongly dislike, distrust, or consider your enemy — even when it's the last thing you want to do.

In short: you're giving credit where credit is genuinely deserved, even to someone you hate.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

The "devil" in this idiom doesn't literally mean the devil from religion. He is used as a symbol — representing the worst possible person: your biggest enemy, your fiercest rival, someone you deeply dislike or consider wicked. If you can be fair even to the devil himself, you are truly being honest and just.

"His due" simply means what he deserves. What is rightfully owed to him. His fair share of credit.

So together, the phrase means: "Even if this person is terrible in my eyes, I will still fairly acknowledge what they have done well."

This idiom carries a very specific emotional flavor — reluctant admiration or grudging respect. It is the feeling of:

"I don't like this person. I really don't want to compliment them. But being honest and fair means I have to admit they did something right."

This is important. The idiom isn't just about giving compliments. It's about the internal struggle between your negative feelings and your commitment to fairness. When someone uses this phrase, they're signaling: "Set my personal feelings aside — here is the truth."
How It Is Used in Real Life

The phrase usually appears when someone is about to say something positive about a person they normally criticize. It acts as a warning signal before the compliment, letting the listener know: "What I'm about to say is fair, not a sign that I like this person."

Example 1:
"I can't stand my ex-boss, but give the devil his due — he always fought for his team's bonuses."
→ The speaker dislikes the boss but fairly admits the boss did something admirable.

Example 2:
"I disagree with almost everything that politician stands for, but give the devil his due — he kept every single promise he made to voters."
→ Despite opposition, the speaker acknowledges a genuine achievement.

Example 3:
"The movie was poorly written, but give the devil his due, the special effects were absolutely stunning."
→ Notice: "the devil" here isn't even a person — it's being applied to something (the movie) that the speaker is criticizing. The idiom can work this way too.

Example 4 (as a standalone phrase):
"He beat me fair and square. Give the devil his due."
→ Said alone, it means: "I'll admit it. He deserved to win."
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The idiom is very old. It has been found in literature dating back to the 16th century. The great English playwright William Shakespeare used it in his famous play Henry IV, Part 1 (written around 1597), where one character says:

"Give the devil his due" in a context that means: even a bad person can be credited for good things.

The Spanish author Miguel de Cervantes also used a nearly identical idea in Don Quixote (1605), showing that this concept of fairness toward even the worst people was recognized across cultures in that era.

The idiom comes from a broader moral idea rooted in fairness and justice — the idea that everyone, no matter how bad, is owed honest acknowledgement when they do something that truly deserves it. Even in old legal and theological thought, people believed you should give others exactly what they are owed — nothing more, nothing less.
Why the Word "Devil" Makes This Idiom So Powerful

The use of the devil is deliberate and clever. Think about it: the devil is the symbol of ultimate evil. If the rule of fairness applies even to him, then there are truly no exceptions. The idiom uses an extreme to prove a universal point:

True fairness has no favorites and no enemies.

If your fairness only applies to people you like, it isn't fairness at all. Real fairness means applying the same honest standard to everyone — including those you despise.
What This Idiom Says About the Person Using It

When someone uses this phrase, it reveals something admirable about them. It shows they are:

  • Intellectually honest — they don't let personal bias cloud their judgment.
  • Mature — they can separate their feelings from the facts.
  • Fair-minded — they apply the same standard to enemies as to friends.

It takes character to admit something good about someone you dislike. This idiom is the language of that character.
What This Idiom Does NOT Mean

To avoid any confusion, here is what the idiom is not:

  • It does not mean you like the person.
  • It does not mean you agree with the person in general.
  • It does not mean you are forgiving them for anything.
  • It does not mean you are becoming friends with them.

You can give the devil his due and still walk away thinking, "That person is still terrible." The idiom is purely about being fair in one specific moment — nothing more.

These phrases are related in spirit and will help you see the bigger picture:

  • "Credit where credit is due" — A very close cousin. Give recognition to whoever honestly earned it.
  • "Fair is fair" — A simple acknowledgment that fairness must apply equally to everyone.
  • "Grudging respect" — This describes the feeling behind giving the devil his due. Respect that you give unwillingly, because honesty demands it.
  • "Even a broken clock is right twice a day" — Even something that is mostly wrong or bad can occasionally be correct or good.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"Give the devil his due" = Be honest and fair enough to admit when even your worst enemy deserves credit.

That's the whole idiom in one sentence. Whenever you find yourself saying something good about someone you dislike — but saying it because it's genuinely true and deserved — you are giving the devil his due.
6941:
To "give the lie to" something means to prove it is false. When one thing "gives the lie to" another, it directly contradicts it and exposes it as untrue — not just by arguing against it, but by presenting undeniable evidence or reality that makes it collapse.

Think of it this way: the truth walks in and slaps the false claim across the face. That slap is what "gives the lie to" means.

The phrase might look confusing at first because it sounds like someone is giving a lie to someone else. But that is NOT what it means. Here is how to read it:

  • "The lie" = the status of being false, being a lie
  • "Give the lie to" = to hand something the label of "this is a lie" — in other words, to expose and prove it as false

So when we say "X gives the lie to Y," it means:

X is the proof or evidence that exposes Y as false.

X is the thing that reveals the truth. Y is the claim, belief, or statement that turns out to be wrong.

Imagine your friend says: "I never eat junk food."

But then you visit his house and find three empty pizza boxes, five candy wrappers, and a pile of chip bags on his desk.

You could say:

"Those pizza boxes and candy wrappers give the lie to his claim that he never eats junk food."

The physical evidence (pizza boxes, candy wrappers) proves his claim is false. The evidence "gives the lie" to what he said.
More Examples to Cement the Meaning

Here are several examples showing how this idiom works in different situations:

  1. "Her shaking hands gave the lie to her calm, confident voice."

(She spoke calmly, but her shaking hands revealed the truth — she was nervous. Her hands disproved her apparent composure.)

  1. "The muddy boots by the door gave the lie to his story that he had been home all evening."

(He said he stayed home, but the muddy boots proved he had been outside. The boots exposed his lie.)

  1. "The country's rising crime rate gives the lie to the government's claim that its new policies are working."

(The government says things are improving, but the crime statistics prove things are not. The data disproves the official claim.)

  1. "His actions give the lie to his words."

(A very common version of this idiom. He says one thing, but what he actually DOES shows the opposite is true. His behavior contradicts his stated beliefs or promises.)

  1. "The discovery of ancient fossils gave the lie to the long-held belief that those species never existed in that region."

(The fossils were the evidence that proved the old belief was wrong.)
The Two Things That "Give the Lie"

Notice a pattern in the examples above. The thing that "gives the lie" — the thing doing the exposing — is almost always one of these two things:

1. Concrete, observable evidence
Physical proof: muddy boots, empty pizza boxes, scientific data, fossils. These are things you can see, touch, or measure that directly contradict a claim.

2. Someone's actual behavior or actions
What a person does exposes what they say as false. This is the classic "actions speak louder than words" scenario, but expressed with sharper, more precise language.
The Weight and Tone of This Phrase

This is not a casual or everyday phrase. It carries a certain weight and sharpness to it. When you use it, you are not just saying "that's not true" — you are saying "the evidence completely destroys that claim." There is a sense of finality and clarity to it.

It is slightly formal and literary in tone. You will often encounter it in:

  • Serious writing (essays, journalism, literature)
  • Formal speech or debate
  • Well-crafted arguments

You would not typically use it in a casual text message to a friend. You might say it or write it when you want to make a strong, precise, elegant point.

The phrase has an interesting origin. Centuries ago, to "give someone the lie" meant to directly accuse them of lying to their face — and this was considered one of the gravest insults a person could receive. It was so serious that it often led to duels. To publicly say "you lie" to a nobleman or a gentleman was an act that demanded a violent response.

Over time, the phrase evolved. Instead of accusing a person of lying, people began using it to describe when evidence or reality itself exposes a claim as false. The person disappeared from the phrase, and it became the more abstract, intellectual tool we use today — where facts, behavior, or evidence "give the lie to" statements and beliefs.

You might wonder: why not just say "disprove" or "contradict" or "prove false"? All of those work perfectly fine. But "give the lie to" does something slightly different:

  • "Disprove" is neutral and technical.
  • "Contradict" means to go against, but doesn't necessarily mean one side is lying.
  • "Give the lie to" carries the implication that the original claim was not just wrong, but deceptive — that it deserved to be exposed. It feels more pointed, more decisive. It suggests that the truth has stepped in and settled the matter.

QuestionAnswer
What does it mean?To prove something is false; to expose a claim as untrue
Who does the exposing?Usually evidence, facts, behavior, or observable reality
What gets exposed?A claim, a statement, a belief, or a story
What is the tone?Formal, sharp, literary, decisive
How to use it?"X gives the lie to Y" — where X is the proof and Y is the false claim
One Final Tip for Using This Idiom

Always remember the structure:

[The evidence/proof/behavior] + gives the lie to + [the claim/statement/belief]

  • ✅ "His lavish lifestyle gives the lie to his claims of poverty."
  • ✅ "The new research gives the lie to that popular myth."
  • ❌ "He gives the lie to me." ← This sounds like the old archaic usage (accusing someone of lying) and would confuse modern readers. Avoid it unless you are writing historical fiction.

Stick to using it to describe how evidence or reality disproves a claim, and you will use it correctly every single time.
6942: "Give up the ghost" means to die, or more broadly, to stop working or functioning permanently. The key idea is always finality — something or someone has come to a complete and permanent end, with no return.

To truly understand this idiom, you need to know what the word "ghost" meant centuries ago.

Today, we think of a ghost as a spooky spirit floating through haunted houses. But the old English and Biblical meaning of the word "ghost" (from the Old English word gāst) simply meant a person's soul or spirit — the invisible life-force believed to live inside every human being.

The ancient belief was this: when a person dies, their soul leaves the body. So "giving up the ghost" literally meant releasing your soul from your body — in other words, dying.

This exact phrase appears in the King James Bible (1611), one of the most influential books in the English language. For example, in the Gospel of John (19:30), when describing the death of Jesus, it says:

"He bowed his head, and gave up the ghost."

It also appears in the books of Genesis, Job, and Acts. Because the Bible was read aloud to millions of people for centuries, this phrase became deeply embedded in the English language and eventually moved beyond religious writing into everyday speech.
The Two Main Ways It's Used Today

1. When a Person Dies

This is the original, literal meaning. When someone says a person "gave up the ghost," they mean that person died.

Examples:

  • "After a long battle with illness, the old general finally gave up the ghost."
  • "The last survivor of the original crew gave up the ghost at the age of 103."

Important tone note: When used about a person's death, the phrase carries a soft, poetic, and dignified tone. It's not harsh or rude. It often suggests the person struggled for a while and then died peacefully or inevitably. You would use it in writing, storytelling, or formal speech — not typically in a casual text message to a friend.

2. When a Machine, Object, or System Stops Working Forever

This is the modern, extended meaning — and it's very commonly used today. When a machine "gives up the ghost," it has broken down completely and cannot be repaired or used anymore. It has reached the end of its life.

Examples:

  • "My old car finally gave up the ghost on the highway — I had to buy a new one."
  • "The printer gave up the ghost right before the deadline. It was completely dead."
  • "Our ancient air conditioner gave up the ghost in the middle of summer."

Tone note: When used about machines or objects, the phrase is lighter and even slightly humorous — almost as if you're joking that the machine had a soul and it flew away. People say it with a small smile, a little frustrated but not devastated.

3. When a Person Stops Trying (Gives Up on an Effort)

Less commonly, the phrase can also mean that a person or organization has decided to stop trying — they've abandoned a plan, a fight, or an effort for good.

Examples:

  • "After three failed attempts to climb the mountain, the team gave up the ghost and turned back."
  • "The small bookshop gave up the ghost after struggling to compete with online retailers for years."

Here, the meaning blends "dying" with "quitting." The effort itself has "died."
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

The phrase always implies total and permanent finality. This is what separates it from simply saying "give up" or "stop working."

Consider the difference:

  • "My phone stopped working" → it might be fixable.
  • "My phone gave up the ghost" → it is gone. Forever. Done. There is no fixing it.

This sense of irreversibility is the heart of the idiom. Whatever gave up the ghost is not coming back.

• It does not mean to believe in ghosts or see a ghost.
  • It does not mean to feel scared or frightened.
  • It does not mean a temporary pause or breakdown — it must be permanent.
  • It does not mean someone or something simply quit halfway through something trivial. It usually applies to longer struggles that finally reach a definitive end.
How Formal or Informal Is It?

This idiom sits in the middle ground:

  • It is literary and slightly formal when used about a person's death.
  • It is casual and conversational when used about machines or failed plans.
  • It is never rude or offensive — unlike some other idioms for death (like "kick the bucket," which is blunt and irreverent).

You can use it in both writing and speech without worrying about offending anyone.

"Give up the ghost" comes from an old belief that the soul leaves the body at death. It originally meant to die, and today it also means a machine, plan, or effort has permanently stopped functioning. The phrase always signals a final, irreversible end — and carries a tone that is poetic for death, and gently humorous for broken objects.
6943: "Give vent to" means to express or release a strong emotion that has been building up inside you — especially when you finally let it out openly.
Understanding It Through the Root Word: "Vent"

To truly understand this idiom, you first need to understand what a vent is in the physical world.

A vent is an opening or a hole through which trapped air, gas, steam, or heat can escape. Think about:

  • The vent on a chimney — hot smoke builds up inside, and the vent lets it escape into the open air.
  • The pressure valve on a pressure cooker — steam builds up inside the pot, and the valve releases it so the pot doesn't explode.

Now apply this same idea to human emotions.

Just like heat or steam, emotions can build up inside a person over time. Anger, frustration, grief, sadness — these feelings don't always come out immediately. Sometimes a person holds them inside, consciously or unconsciously. Then, at some point, they let those feelings out — they express them, release them, pour them out.

That release is exactly what "give vent to" describes.

When you "give vent to" an emotion, you are opening a passage for that emotion to come out of you.
The Full, Precise Definition

"Give vent to" means to openly and freely express a strong inner feeling — particularly one that had been suppressed, held back, or quietly accumulating — by letting it out through words, actions, or behaviour.

The key ideas packed inside this idiom are:

  • The emotion was held inside before.
  • It has been building up with some intensity or pressure.
  • The person finally releases or expresses it — in full, without completely holding back.
Grammatical Structure

The idiom follows this pattern:

Subject + give vent to + (emotion/feeling)

The word "give" changes form depending on the tense:

  • Present: She gives vent to her frustration by shouting.
  • Past: He gave vent to his anger by slamming the door.
  • Future: She will give vent to her grief at the funeral.
  • Continuous: He was giving vent to his disappointment in the letter.

Notice that "to" is a preposition here, so it is always followed by a noun (a naming word for the emotion), not a verb.

✅ Correct: give vent to her anger
❌ Incorrect: give vent to being angry
The Emotions It Is Typically Used With

This idiom is almost always used with strong emotions — not mild or casual feelings. The most common ones are:

  • Anger / rage / fury
  • Frustration
  • Grief / sorrow
  • Feelings / emotions (used generally)
  • Displeasure / indignation
  • Resentment
  • Joy / delight (less common, but possible)

You would not normally say "she gave vent to her slight preference for tea" — the idiom carries a sense of emotional weight and intensity.
Real-World Example Sentences

Here are rich, clear examples showing the idiom in action:

  1. After weeks of being ignored by his manager, he finally gave vent to his frustration in a long, strongly-worded email.

(He had been holding his frustration inside for weeks. He let it all out in the email.)

  1. At the funeral, she gave vent to her grief and wept openly for the first time since his death.

(She had been keeping her grief inside. The funeral was where she finally released it.)

  1. The angry crowd gave vent to their feelings by chanting and holding protest signs.

(The crowd expressed the emotions that had been building up inside them.)

  1. He wrote a fierce poem to give vent to his sense of injustice.

(He used writing as the channel to release his strong inner feeling.)

  1. She gave vent to her delight by jumping up and hugging everyone in the room.

(Here, even a positive emotion — delight — was released fully and openly.)
The Crucial Nuance: Suppression Before Expression

This is the most important thing to understand about this idiom.

It is not simply a fancy way of saying "to feel an emotion." It carries a specific implication: the emotion existed inside the person before it came out. There is a sense of something being held back and then finally released.

Compare:

  • "He felt angry." — This just tells us about an emotion.
  • "He gave vent to his anger." — This tells us he expressed anger that had been building inside him. He let it out.

This is why the pressure-valve image is so perfect. The steam was always there. Giving vent is the moment the valve opens.
Tone and Register (Formal or Informal?)

"Give vent to" is slightly formal and literary. You will see it more often in:

  • Written English (books, newspapers, formal letters)
  • Speeches or structured conversation
  • Literature and journalism

In casual, everyday speech, people tend to say things like:

  • "I just need to vent."
  • "She let it all out."
  • "He blew off some steam."

So if you are writing an essay, a letter, or a formal piece, "give vent to" fits beautifully. In a casual conversation with a friend, people are less likely to use the full form.
Similar Expressions (Synonyms)

These idioms and phrases carry a very similar meaning:

  • To vent (one's feelings/anger) — She vented her anger at him. (More casual)
  • To let out — He let out his frustration.
  • To pour out — She poured out her feelings.
  • To express — He expressed his displeasure. (More neutral, less emotional intensity)
  • To blow off steam — She went for a run to blow off steam. (Very informal)
  • To unleash — He unleashed his rage. (More intense, dramatic)
  • To air (one's grievances) — She aired her grievances at the meeting.

Among all of these, "give vent to" is the most formal and carries the clearest image of internal pressure being released through an outlet.
What "Give Vent to" Does NOT Mean

Let's clear up any possible confusion:

  • It does not mean to simply feel an emotion quietly inside.
  • It does not mean to cause someone else to feel an emotion.
  • It does not mean a small, polite mention of a feeling. It implies a real, noticeable release.
  • It is not always negative — though it is most commonly used with negative emotions, you can technically give vent to joy, excitement, or delight too.
One Final Summary

Imagine a person who has been silently dealing with a difficult situation for a long time. They haven't said a word. The feelings pile up inside them like steam in a sealed pot. Then one day — through tears, words, a letter, a shout, or even a painting — they let it all out.

That moment of release is what it means to "give vent to" an emotion.

It is the act of opening the inner door and letting the built-up feeling finally walk out into the open world.
6944:
To give voice to something means to express it, say it out loud, or put it into words — especially when that thing was previously unspoken, hidden, or difficult to communicate.

Think of it this way: a feeling, idea, or concern can exist inside a person (or inside a group of people) in silence. It is real, but it has no "voice" — no words, no sound, no public expression. When someone gives voice to it, they take that silent thing and bring it into the open by expressing it clearly.

The expression works because of a simple, powerful metaphor:

Voice = the ability to be heard.

If something has no voice, it is silent — it exists, but the world cannot hear it. To give it a voice is to give it the power to be heard. You are acting like a speaker for something that had no speaker before.

This is why the expression feels slightly more powerful and meaningful than simply saying "say" or "talk about." It carries the sense that something important was waiting to be expressed, and now it finally is.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Expressing Your Own Feelings or Thoughts

You can use "give voice to" when a person finally puts their own inner feelings or thoughts into words — especially feelings they had been holding inside for a long time.

Examples:

  • "He finally gave voice to the anger he had felt for years."

(He had been angry for a long time, but he had never said it openly. Now he did.)

  • "In her diary, she gave voice to her deepest fears."

(She wrote down her fears — fears that had been living silently inside her.)

  • "The artist gave voice to his grief through his paintings."

(He did not speak literally, but his paintings expressed the grief he was carrying inside.)

Notice in that last example something important: the thing you give voice to does not always have to come out as spoken words. A painting, a song, a poem, or a piece of writing can also "give voice to" a feeling. The key idea is expression, not necessarily literal speech.

2. Speaking on Behalf of Others

This is a very common and important use. When a person or organization "gives voice to" a group of people, they are representing those people's feelings, concerns, or perspectives — speaking for those who cannot speak for themselves, or who have not been heard.

Examples:

  • "The journalist gave voice to the communities that the government had ignored."

(Those communities had real concerns, but no one was listening to them. The journalist spoke up for them and made the world hear their concerns.)

  • "This book gives voice to women who lived in silence for centuries."

(The book expresses the experiences and perspectives of women from the past, who never had the opportunity to tell their own stories.)

  • "The protest gave voice to millions of frustrated citizens."

(The protest expressed — publicly and loudly — what millions of people were feeling inside but had no platform to say.)

This second use is especially powerful because it often involves the weak, the forgotten, the ignored, or the oppressed. The expression carries a sense of justice and compassion — someone is making sure that important voices are not lost.
The Key Hidden Ingredient: Something Was Previously Unspoken

This is what makes "give voice to" special and different from simply "express" or "say."

When you use this expression, there is almost always an implied sense that the thing being expressed already existed but was waiting to be spoken. The feeling was real. The concern was real. The experience was real. But it had been trapped in silence — because of fear, lack of opportunity, lack of power, or simply because no one had found the right words yet.

"Give voice to" is the act of unlocking that silence.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She said she was unhappy." → Simple. Neutral. She spoke.
  • "She gave voice to her unhappiness." → This implies the unhappiness had been building inside her, unspoken, for a while. Now it finally came out.

The second sentence is richer and more meaningful because of that hidden implication.

"Give voice to" is a slightly formal and literary expression. You will see it often in:

  • News articles and journalism
  • Books, essays, and literary criticism
  • Political speeches
  • Documentary films
  • Academic writing
  • Thoughtful conversations

It is not wrong to use it in everyday speech, but it sounds elevated and intentional — the kind of expression a writer or speaker uses when they want to be precise and thoughtful.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Similar ExpressionHow "Give Voice To" Is Different

"Express" is more neutral and broad. You can express joy, express a thought, express a preference. "Give voice to" implies something deeper — that the thing being expressed had been silent and needed a spokesperson or outlet.

"Say" is even more neutral — it just means words came out of your mouth. "Give voice to" implies meaning, weight, and intention behind those words.

"Speak for" is close to the second use of "give voice to" (representing others), but "give voice to" is slightly more poetic and emphasizes the act of bringing something into the light of expression.

"Put into words" is similar, but "give voice to" often works on a bigger scale — it can apply to entire communities, historical experiences, or widespread feelings, not just a single personal thought.

"Give voice to" means to express something that was previously unspoken — whether that is your own inner feeling, idea, or concern, or the feelings and concerns of others who have not been heard. It carries a sense of importance and purpose: you are not just speaking, you are making something heard that deserved to be heard.
A Few More Sentences to Cement Your Understanding

• "The novel gives voice to the struggles of immigrants who are rarely represented in literature."
  • "She struggled for years to give voice to the trauma she had experienced as a child."
  • "Music can give voice to emotions that ordinary words simply cannot capture."
  • "The union leader gave voice to the workers' demand for fair wages."
  • "His speech finally gave voice to what everyone in the room had been thinking but was afraid to say."

In every single one of these examples, notice the pattern: something real and important existed in silence → someone or something expressed it → now it can be heard.

That is "give voice to."
6945:
"Give-and-take" describes a process where both sides of a relationship, discussion, or situation give something up and receive something in return. Neither side gets everything they want. Neither side walks away empty-handed. Both sides bend a little — and because of that bending, something good becomes possible for everyone.

The word is almost self-explanatory if you take it literally: you give (you let go of something, you make a concession) and you take (you receive something back). The beauty of the word is that it always implies both directions at once. It is never one-way.

Meaning 1 — Mutual Compromise

This is the most common meaning. "Give-and-take" refers to the process of two or more people making mutual concessions — each one agreeing to give up some part of what they want, so that everyone can move forward together, reach an agreement, or keep a relationship healthy.

The keyword is mutual. Both sides give. Both sides take. This is what separates give-and-take from simply "giving in" (which is one-sided — only one person sacrifices everything).

Examples:

  • "A good marriage requires give-and-take."
  • "The deal between the two companies was the result of give-and-take."
  • "Working on a team always involves give-and-take."

In the marriage example, both partners sometimes do what the other needs, even when it is not their first choice. One partner might agree to live in a city they didn't originally prefer; the other might give up a habit the first partner dislikes. Both sacrifice something; both gain something. The balance is what keeps the relationship working.

Meaning 2 — A Lively Back-and-Forth Exchange of Ideas

The second meaning is slightly different. Here, give-and-take refers to an active, flowing, two-way exchange of opinions, ideas, arguments, or even jokes between people — where both sides are fully engaged, responding to each other, pushing back, and building on what the other says.

In this sense, the word is not about compromise. It is about the dynamic quality of a conversation or debate — the fact that it flows in both directions, rather than one person dominating and the other just listening.

Examples:

  • "I really enjoyed the give-and-take of our discussion — we kept questioning each other's ideas."
  • "The give-and-take between the two debaters was exciting to watch."
  • "A great creative session depends on free give-and-take among the team."

In these examples, no one is necessarily "compromising." Instead, everyone is actively participating — speaking and listening, challenging and responding. The conversation has energy in both directions.
The Thread That Connects Both Meanings

Both meanings share the same soul: something flows both ways.

In Meaning 1 — concessions flow both ways.
In Meaning 2 — ideas and responses flow both ways.

"Give-and-take" always implies mutuality, balance, and active participation from both sides. If only one person is giving, or only one person is speaking, that is NOT give-and-take.

This is important to understand clearly:

  • It is not one person always giving while the other always takes. That is exploitation or unfairness — the exact opposite of give-and-take. (In fact, people sometimes say "it's all give and no take" to describe a situation that lacks this balance.)
  • It is not "giving in" or surrendering completely. When you give in, you abandon your position entirely and get nothing back. In give-and-take, you only partially adjust your position, and you receive something in return.
  • It is not a single, one-time event. Give-and-take is typically an ongoing process — something that happens again and again over the course of a relationship, negotiation, or conversation.
  • It is not forced or hostile. It carries a connotation of willingness — both sides are choosing to participate in the exchange.

Give-and-take does not require a perfectly equal split — but it does imply a reasonable balance. If one side consistently gives far more than the other, people would say the give-and-take has broken down. The spirit of the word is fairness and cooperation, not a mathematically precise calculation.
Where You Will Commonly See This Word Used

• Relationships and family life — marriages, friendships, parenting
  • The workplace — teamwork, collaborations, managing disagreements
  • Politics and international affairs — peace talks, negotiations, policy-making
  • Business — deal-making, partnerships, contracts
  • Everyday conversation — any lively, two-sided discussion

Give-and-take (noun): A mutual process where both sides make concessions so that everyone benefits (Meaning 1), or a lively, two-sided exchange of ideas and responses between people (Meaning 2). In every case, the defining quality is the same — things move in both directions, not just one.
6946:
When "given" is used as a preposition, it means "taking into account" or "considering."

It introduces a fact — something true, known, or accepted — and signals that the rest of the sentence is a natural, logical outcome or reaction to that fact.

Think of it as saying: "Here is one important fact. Keep it in mind, because it explains what I'm about to say."

Given the rain, we stayed inside.

This means: Taking into account the fact that it was raining → we stayed inside. The rain is the context. The staying inside is the logical result. "Given" is the bridge between them.

"Given" is not just a filler word. It does a specific, precise job: it links a premise to a conclusion.

  • The part after "given" = the premise (a fact you're treating as established and real)
  • The main part of the sentence = the conclusion (what logically follows from that premise)

Given his experience, he handled the crisis well.

Here, "his experience" is the established premise. "He handled the crisis well" is the conclusion that flows logically from it. You're essentially saying: "Because we know he is experienced, his calm handling of the crisis makes complete sense."

This is what makes "given" feel slightly formal and precise — it is presenting something as a settled, undeniable starting point, not as a guess or a maybe.

You will see "given" appear in two slightly different structures, but they mean exactly the same thing.

Form 1: "Given" + noun or noun phrase

Given the evidence, the verdict was clear.
Given her age, she's incredibly fast.
Given the circumstances, you did well.

Form 2: "Given that" + full clause (subject + verb)

Given that the evidence was strong, the verdict was clear.
Given that she is only ten years old, she's incredibly fast.
Given that the circumstances were difficult, you did well.

The only difference is grammar: "given" alone is followed by a noun phrase, while "given that" is followed by a complete clause. Choose whichever fits what you're saying.
The Range of What "Given" Can Do

The core meaning stays the same, but "given" can serve several different purposes depending on the sentence.

1. To explain why something happened

Given how little he studied, his poor result was expected.

The lack of studying explains the poor result. "Given" frames the cause.

2. To justify a decision

Given the high price, we chose a different option.

The high price is the reason behind the decision. "Given" presents it as the rational basis.

3. To make a surprising result feel understandable

Given how nervous she was, she performed remarkably well.

The nervousness sets up what you'd expect (a bad performance). "She performed remarkably well" is the surprising reality. "Given" makes the surprise meaningful — you understand the full weight of her achievement only because you're told about her nerves.

4. To state a condition under which something is possible or true

Given enough time, anyone can learn a new language.

Here, "given" introduces a condition (enough time) — not necessarily a current fact, but a premise being assumed. The meaning is: "Assuming this condition is in place, the following is true." This is similar to "if," but feels more like a settled assumption than a pure hypothetical.

These words are often used in similar ways, but they are not identical.

Given vs. If

"If" introduces something uncertain or hypothetical — something that may or may not be true.
"Given" treats the thing as real, established, or accepted.

If it rains, we will stay inside. — We don't know yet whether it will rain.
Given the rain, we stayed inside. — It did rain. That is the accepted fact.

So "given" is more grounded in reality. "If" leaves the door open; "given" walks through it.

Given vs. Because

"Because" directly states a cause: A happened because of B.
"Given" is slightly more indirect — it presents a context or premise, not just a cause.

We stayed inside because it was raining. — Straightforward cause and effect.
Given the rain, we stayed inside. — Slightly more formal; treats the rain as a premise you're reasoning from.

In many cases they overlap, but "given" carries a more logical, reasoned tone.

Given vs. Since

"Since" is the closest word to "given" in everyday English, and the two are often interchangeable when "since" means "considering" or "because."

Since it was raining, we stayed inside.
Given the rain, we stayed inside.

Both work. The difference is subtle: "given" feels slightly more formal and precise, and it places slightly more emphasis on the fact being a fixed, undeniable premise. "Since" is more casual and natural in spoken conversation.

Given vs. Considering

These are almost identical in meaning. "Considering" feels slightly more evaluative — as if you are actively weighing the fact. "Given" feels more like stating a fixed premise.

Considering how busy she was, she did an excellent job.
Given how busy she was, she did an excellent job.

Both are correct and nearly the same. "Given" is just a touch more formal.

"Given" almost always appears at the beginning of a sentence or clause, introducing the premise before the main point.

Given the delay, we rescheduled the meeting.

Occasionally, you'll see it at the end of a sentence, though this is less common.

Her frustration made sense, given the situation.

Both positions are correct. The front position is more common because it mirrors the logic: you state the premise first, then the conclusion. But placing it at the end works when you want to state the main point first and then add the explanation.

Whenever you see or hear "given" used as a preposition, replace it in your head with:

"Taking into account the fact that..." or "In light of..."

If the sentence still makes sense with that replacement, then "given" is being used as a preposition, and you understand it correctly.

Given the noise, I couldn't concentrate.
→ Taking into account the noise, I couldn't concentrate. ✓

That mental test works every single time.

What makes "given" feel precise and slightly formal is that it borrows from the language of logic and mathematics — where a "given" is an established fact you start from before drawing conclusions. When you use "given" in everyday language, you carry that same spirit: you are saying "this fact is not in question — now let's reason forward from it." That is why "given" often appears in arguments, explanations, analysis, and professional writing. It signals clear, logical thinking.
6947:
When someone is "given to" something, it means they have a deep, habitual tendency or inclination toward that thing. It describes a characteristic that someone keeps showing, again and again — almost like it is built into them.

Think of it this way: the word given here does not mean "handed over." Instead, it means something closer to disposed or inclined. You are saying that a person is, by their nature or habit, strongly pulled toward a certain behavior or quality.

The simplest way to understand it:

"Given to" = has a habit of / tends to / is prone to

"Given to" almost always appears in this pattern:

[Someone] is / was given to + [a noun or a verb ending in -ing]

Examples:

  • She is given to gossip.
  • He was given to sudden outbursts of laughter.
  • The professor is given to rambling during lectures.
  • Children are often given to daydreaming.

The subject is always a person (or a group of people). The thing after "given to" is always the habit or tendency being described.
The Connotation — What Feeling Does It Carry?

This is important. "Given to" most often describes a habit that is:

  • a personal weakness or flaw ("given to lying," "given to self-pity"),
  • a quirk or unusual characteristic ("given to sudden silences"), or
  • something excessive or difficult to control ("given to fits of rage").

It is not usually used for a deliberate, positive skill. You would not naturally say "She is given to helping people" — that sounds odd. But you could say "She is given to worrying too much about others," because now it is a compulsive habit.

That said, it is sometimes used in a neutral or even gentle way:

  • "He is given to long walks in the evening." — This is not negative at all; it simply describes a habitual preference.

The key idea is always habit and tendency, not a one-time action. It describes who someone is, not just what someone did once.

Negative / weakness:

  • "The manager is given to making promises he cannot keep." (He habitually overpromises.)
  • "She was given to jealousy whenever her husband spoke to another woman." (She had a persistent, recurring jealousy.)
  • "He is given to exaggeration — you cannot take his stories too literally." (Exaggerating is his habit.)

Neutral / quirk:

  • "My grandfather was given to humming old folk songs while he worked." (It was his characteristic habit.)
  • "The writer was given to long periods of isolation before finishing a book." (A recurring pattern in her behavior.)

Slightly negative / excessive:

  • "Young politicians are sometimes given to grand speeches that mean very little." (They tend to do this habitually.)
How It Differs From Similar Phrases

Several phrases are close in meaning, so it helps to know the differences:

"Prone to" — very similar, but it leans more toward vulnerability or susceptibility, especially to something bad.

  • "He is prone to infections." (His body is vulnerable.)
  • "She is prone to anxiety." (She easily suffers from it.)

"Given to" is more about a habitual behavior or personal inclination, while "prone to" often feels more like something that happens to you (illness, accidents, emotional attacks).

"Inclined to" — this means having a preference or leaning toward something, but it sounds more deliberate and less habitual.

  • "I am inclined to agree with you." (I lean toward agreeing — right now, in this situation.)

"Given to" is a stronger, more permanent habit. "Inclined to" can be temporary.

"Tends to" — the most casual and everyday equivalent. If "given to" is a formal suit, "tends to" is jeans and a t-shirt.

  • "He tends to talk too much." = "He is given to talking too much." — same meaning, different register.

"Apt to" — means likely to, sometimes used for habits, sometimes just for predictions.

  • "She is apt to forget." (She tends to forget / she is likely to forget.)
A Special Related Phrase: "Given to Understand"

There is a second, separate idiom that uses "given to" in a completely different way. You will hear it in formal or polite English:

"I was given to understand that..."

This means: I was led to believe / I was informed (indirectly) that...

It suggests that someone told you something, but perhaps not directly or officially.

  • "I was given to understand that the meeting had been cancelled." (Someone implied it or I heard it indirectly.)
  • "She was given to understand that the job was hers." (She was made to believe it, though it was never stated outright.)

This phrase is particularly common when the information turned out to be wrong, or when the speaker is being polite about a misunderstanding:

  • "I was given to understand you would be joining us for dinner." (Someone told me you would come — are you not coming?)
The Tone and Register — When Is "Given to" Used?

"Given to" is slightly formal and literary. You will find it more often in:

  • written English (essays, novels, journalism),
  • formal speech or descriptions of character,
  • slightly old-fashioned or careful, considered language.

In everyday casual conversation, people usually say "tends to" or "has a habit of" instead. But "given to" is not rare or archaic — it is used regularly in good writing and educated speech.

One last thing: do not confuse the idiomatic "given to" with the plain, literal use of the words.

  • "The trophy was given to the winner." — Here, "given" simply means handed/awarded, and "to" points to the recipient. This is just the verb give in passive voice. There is no idiom here.

The idiomatic "given to" always describes a person's habitual nature, and it always follows be (is, was, are, were, etc.):

  • ✅ "He is given to brooding." (idiom — habitual tendency)
  • ✅ "The prize was given to her." (literal — she received it)

The meaning is entirely different, and context makes it obvious.

"Given to" means habitually inclined toward something — it describes a deep, recurring tendency in a person's character or behavior, and it is most often used for quirks, weaknesses, or compulsive habits.
6948:
Step 1: What Does "Given to" Mean?

When we say someone is "given to" something, we mean it is a habit or tendency of theirs. It means they do it naturally, regularly, and almost automatically — often without even realizing it.

Think of it like this:

  • "She is given to long walks at night." → She tends to take long walks at night. It's her habit.
  • "He is given to sudden mood changes." → He has a tendency to change moods suddenly.

So "given to" simply means: this person has a natural leaning or recurring habit toward something.

It does not mean they were "given" something like a gift. It's a different use of the word "given." Think of it as: their personality has been given over to this tendency.
Step 2: What Is "Hyperbole"?

Hyperbole (pronounced: hy-PER-buh-lee) is a figure of speech where someone exaggerates massively and dramatically — far beyond what is literally true — in order to make a point, create emphasis, or express strong emotion.

The key thing to understand is that hyperbole is not meant to be taken literally. Both the speaker and the listener understand that it's an exaggeration. The goal is to create a vivid, powerful impression, not to state a factual truth.

Everyday Examples of Hyperbole

These are phrases you've almost certainly heard before:

  • "I've told you a million times!" → The speaker hasn't literally said it a million times. They mean they've said it many times and are frustrated.
  • "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse." → They can't eat a horse. They just mean they're very hungry.
  • "This bag weighs a ton!" → The bag doesn't weigh a ton. It just feels very heavy.
  • "I've been waiting forever." → They haven't waited forever — maybe twenty minutes. But it felt endless.
  • "She's the nicest person on the entire planet." → They haven't met everyone on the planet. They simply mean she's extremely nice.
  • "I could sleep for a thousand years." → They mean they're exhausted, not that they literally want to sleep for centuries.

Notice how in every case, the exaggeration is so extreme that no reasonable person thinks it's meant literally. That's the defining feature of hyperbole.
Step 3: Where Does the Word "Hyperbole" Come From?

The word comes from ancient Greek:

  • "Hyper" = over, beyond, above
  • "Ballein" = to throw

So hyperbole literally means "to throw beyond" — to throw a statement far beyond the limits of reality. Imagine throwing a ball, but throwing it so hard and so far that it goes miles past its target. That's what hyperbole does with the truth — it throws it way past the normal boundary.

The word has been part of English since at least the 15th century, borrowed through Latin from Greek.
Step 4: Putting It Together — "Given to Hyperbole"

Now that you understand both parts, the full expression is simple:

"Given to hyperbole" means someone has a habit or natural tendency to exaggerate wildly and dramatically when they speak or write.

It's a way of describing a person's communication style — specifically, that their default mode is to overstate things enormously.

Examples of the Expression in Use

  • "My uncle is given to hyperbole — according to him, every meal he cooks is 'the greatest dish in human history.'"
    His uncle constantly and dramatically overstates how good his cooking is.
  • "The coach was given to hyperbole, calling every practice session 'the most grueling workout any athlete has ever endured.'"
    The coach has a habit of exaggerating the intensity of workouts.
  • "As a writer, she was given to hyperbole — a simple rainstorm in her stories became 'a sky splitting apart at the seams.'"
    Her writing style is consistently and heavily exaggerated.
  • "Don't take him too literally; he's given to hyperbole. When he says a film is 'unwatchable garbage,' he usually just means he mildly disliked it."
    You have to mentally "dial down" what he says because he always overstates his reactions.
Step 5: The Tone of the Expression — Is It a Criticism?

This is important. When someone says a person is "given to hyperbole," the tone can be:

Mildly critical or skeptical. It often implies that the person exaggerates so much that you can't fully trust the scale of what they say. You have to take their statements with a grain of salt. It suggests a minor flaw — they're not lying, but they're not being precise either.

Affectionately observational. Sometimes it's said with a smile, as a charming quirk of someone's personality. A storyteller who is "given to hyperbole" can be fun, lively, and entertaining.

Neutral or descriptive. In literary or academic contexts, it can simply describe someone's style without judgment.

The context and tone of voice (or writing) tell you which one is meant. But in most everyday usage, there is a slight implication that the person overdoes it and that their exaggerations should be mentally adjusted before being believed.
Step 6: Hyperbole vs. Lying — A Critical Distinction

You might wonder: if someone exaggerates, aren't they lying? The answer is no, and here's why:

A lie is a deliberate false statement where the speaker wants the listener to believe something untrue as if it were fact.

Hyperbole is an exaggeration that both parties understand is not literally true. No one really believes the speaker waited "forever" or could "eat a horse." The exaggeration is a tool for emotional expression, not deception.

Think of it this way: if you said "I've been waiting forever" and someone replied "Actually, it's only been fifteen minutes," they've missed the point entirely. The exaggeration was not meant as a fact claim — it was a way of expressing that the wait felt long and frustrating.

So someone who is "given to hyperbole" is not a liar. They are simply someone whose natural impulse is to dramatize and amplify their language for effect.
Step 7: Why Do People Use Hyperbole?

People exaggerate for several natural, human reasons:

To express strong emotion. When feelings are intense, normal words can feel inadequate. Saying "I was a bit upset" doesn't capture how you felt — so you say "I was absolutely devastated."

To be vivid and memorable. Exaggerated descriptions stick in the mind. "The line was long" is forgettable. "The line stretched to the moon" creates a picture.

For humor. Much of comedy relies on hyperbole. Taking something small and blowing it up to ridiculous proportions is a classic comedic technique.

For emphasis. Hyperbole signals to the listener: pay attention to this, because it's important or intense.

Out of habit or personality. Some people are simply naturally dramatic communicators. They don't consciously choose to exaggerate — it's just how they express themselves. These are the people we describe as "given to hyperbole."
Step 8: Hyperbole in Literature and Writing

Hyperbole isn't just found in everyday speech — it's a celebrated literary device used by some of the greatest writers in history.

  • In Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, Romeo says Juliet's beauty makes the stars look dim by comparison. That's hyperbole — used to show the depth of his love.
  • In tall tales and folk stories, heroes perform impossible feats (Paul Bunyan dug the Grand Canyon with his axe). The exaggeration creates a mythic, larger-than-life quality.
  • In advertising, hyperbole is everywhere: "The best burger ever made," "You'll never eat anywhere else again."

When we say a writer is "given to hyperbole," we mean their writing style regularly features this kind of dramatic over-the-top expression as a recurring characteristic.
Step 9: How to Recognize If Someone Is "Given to Hyperbole"

Here are signs that someone has this tendency:

  • Their descriptions consistently involve extreme words: best ever, worst in history, a million times, forever, never, always, the entire world.
  • When they tell stories, the details are always slightly (or wildly) more dramatic than seems plausible.
  • You find yourself mentally halving or dividing their claims to get to the likely reality.
  • They react to minor things with extreme language — a slightly long wait becomes "an eternity," a moderately good meal becomes "the best thing I've ever tasted."
  • Other people around them often gently say things like "Well, it wasn't that bad…"
Step 10: Quick Summary

ConceptSimple Meaning
  • "Given to" = has a habit or natural tendency toward something.
  • "Hyperbole" = wild, dramatic exaggeration not meant to be taken literally.
  • "Given to hyperbole" = a person whose natural habit is to express themselves through extreme, dramatic exaggeration.
  • It's not the same as lying — the exaggeration is understood by all parties.
  • The tone is usually mildly critical (suggesting you can't take them at face value) but can also be affectionate or neutral.
  • People use hyperbole to convey emotion, humor, vividness, and emphasis.
One Final Image to Lock It In

Imagine a friend who comes back from a camping trip and says:

"It was the coldest night in the history of the universe. I was buried under seventeen blankets and I still nearly froze to death. I must have woken up a billion times. I will never go camping again as long as I live."

It was probably just a chilly night, they had two blankets, woke up a few times, and will likely go camping again next summer.

That person is given to hyperbole.

They're not lying. They're not trying to trick you. They just naturally communicate in extremes — and once you know that about them, you learn to translate their dramatic language into the more modest reality it actually describes.
6949: The core meaning is simple: glabrous means naturally smooth and completely free of hair, fuzz, bristles, or any tiny hair-like outgrowths on a surface. If something is glabrous, its surface has no such projections on it whatsoever — it is clean, smooth, and bare by nature.

This is the most important nuance to understand. Glabrous doesn't just mean hairless. It means inherently, naturally hairless — as in, the surface was never meant to have hair in the first place, or it belongs to a type that simply grows that way.

A shaved human head is not glabrous — it was made smooth artificially. But the palm of your hand is glabrous — it naturally has no hair follicles at all. That's a crucial distinction. The word describes a natural characteristic of a surface, not a result of trimming, shaving, or removing.
Where You'll Most Commonly See This Word

1. In Botany (plants)

This is where you'll encounter "glabrous" the most. Botanists use it to describe leaves, stems, or fruits whose surfaces are perfectly smooth — with no tiny hairs (called trichomes) at all.

For example: a glabrous leaf feels slick and clean when you run your finger across it. Compare that to a fuzzy peach skin or the underside of a mullein leaf, which are covered in fine, soft hairs — those are the opposite of glabrous. If you look at plant field guides or scientific descriptions, you'll frequently see phrases like "leaves glabrous above", which simply tells you the top surface of that leaf is smooth and hairless.

2. In Medicine and Anatomy (human skin)

Doctors and anatomists use "glabrous skin" to refer to specific areas of the human body that are naturally hairless. The clearest examples are:

  • The palms of your hands
  • The soles of your feet
  • Your lips
  • Your fingertips

These areas don't just happen to be without hair — they are structurally built without hair follicles. Glabrous skin also tends to be thicker, has distinct ridges (like your fingerprints), and is packed with more touch-sensitive nerve endings than hairy skin. Dermatologists will talk about glabrous skin when discussing conditions like fungal infections, because certain fungi behave differently depending on whether they are on glabrous skin versus hairy skin.

3. In Zoology (animals)

The word is also used to describe animal body parts or entire species that are smooth and lack hair, fur, or feather-like structures. A hairless mole rat, for instance, could be described as having a glabrous body surface.

It helps to be clear about what the word does not mean, because beginners sometimes conflate it with related ideas:

  • It does not mean soft. A glabrous surface could be hard (like a smooth seed pod) or soft (like your lips).
  • It does not mean shiny. A glabrous surface can appear shiny or lustrous, but the word itself says nothing about shine — only about the absence of hair-like structures.
  • It does not mean smooth in a general sense (like a polished floor). It is specifically about the absence of hair, bristles, or fuzz — not about the absence of bumps or ridges. Your fingerprints have ridges, yet your fingertips are still considered glabrous.

Knowing the antonyms will help cement the meaning. In botany especially, several words describe surfaces that are not glabrous:

  • Pubescent — covered with fine, soft, short hairs (like the skin of a peach)
  • Hirsute — covered with coarser, longer, stiffer hairs
  • Tomentose — densely covered with matted, woolly hairs (like the underside of some oak leaves)
  • Ciliate — fringed with hair-like projections along the edges

All of these stand in contrast to glabrous, which sits at the far end of the spectrum: zero hair or hair-like growth.
A Simple Test to Remember It

Ask yourself: Does this surface have any hair, fuzz, bristles, or tiny projections on it — and is it naturally built that way?

  • If yes to hair/fuzz → Not glabrous.
  • If no hair/fuzz, and that's its natural state → Glabrous.

Your palm? Glabrous. A smooth, shiny green apple? Glabrous. A cactus? Definitely not glabrous. A rose stem? Not glabrous (it has prickles). A freshly shaved chin? Not glabrous — because hair follicles are still there underneath.

Glabrous is a precise scientific adjective meaning naturally smooth and free of hair or hair-like surface structures. It is most at home in botany, medicine, and zoology, where exact surface descriptions matter. The word always implies that the smoothness is an inherent property of the surface — not something created artificially. When you see it, you can immediately picture a clean, bare, smooth surface — a leaf without a single hair on it, a palm that never had one.
